title: Symmetric Space Learning for Combinatorial Generalization
claim: Learned symmetries stay closed within the observed region, so they cannot extend to unseen data beyond it.
layout: single circular panel, top-to-bottom, observed vs unseen regions split by wavy boundary
description: A large gray circle represents the data manifold. A wavy line splits it into a darker upper observed region and a lighter lower unseen region. In the observed region, three red shapes (triangle, diamond, heart) are linked by black curved arrows in a closed cycle, which shows a learned group action that stays inside the observed region. Near the boundary, a smaller cycle of shapes has arrows that cross into the unseen region. Those arrows are marked with black X's, and a faded dashed square sits on the unseen side. The marks show the action is blocked there. Rotated labels read 'Observed region', 'Unseen region' and 'Data manifold'. The eye goes first to the bright red shapes on the gray background.
caption: Since trained group actions should be closed on the observed region, they cannot affect the unseen region.
abstract: Combinatorial generalization (CG)—generalizing to unseen combinations of known semantic factors—remains a grand challenge in machine learning. While symmetry-based methods are promising, they learn from observed data and thus fail at what we term $\textbf{symmetry generalization}$: extending learned symmetries to novel data. We tackle this by proposing a novel framework that endows the latent space with the structure of a $\textbf{symmetric space}$, a class of manifolds whose geometric properties provide a principled way to extend these symmetries. Our method operates in two steps: first, it imposes this structure by learning the underlying algebraic properties via the $\textbf{Cartan decomposition}$ of a learnable Lie algebra. Second, it uses $\textbf{geodesic symmetry}$ as a powerful self-supervisory signal to ensure this learned structure extrapolates from observed samples to unseen ones. A detailed analysis on a synthetic dataset validates our geometric claims, and experiments on standard CG benchmarks show our method significantly outperforms existing approaches.
